title: Usha Rani vs Shaista Khan on 28 October, 2025
full_text: Usha Rani vs Shaista Khan on 28 October, 2025 IN THE COURT OF Ms. AASTHA SHARMA, LD. JMFC (N.I. Act)-03, SOUTH-EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: DELHI Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan CC No. 619337/2016 U/S 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1. CNR number DLSE020018782013 2. Name of the complainant Ms. Usha Rani W/o Late Sh. Ashok Kumar R/o RZ-822, Gali no.23, Tuglakabad Extn., New Delhi-110019. 3. Name of the accused person(s), parentage & Smt. Shaista Khan residential address W/o Sh. Rafique Khan @ Bittu R/o RZ - 261, 1st Floor, Gali no. 19, Tughlakabad Extn., New Delhi-110019. CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 1 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 15:59:44 +0530 Also at: 802/23, Top Floor, Tughlakabad Extn., New Delhi. 4. Offence complained of or proved U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 5. Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order Acquittal 7. Date of judgment/order 28.10.2025 Date of Institution: 24.01.2013 Date of Reserving Judgment/Order: 10.09.2025 Date of Pronouncement of Judgment/Order: 28.10.2025 ARGUING COUNSELS: Ld. Counsel for the complainant: Sh. Harsh Chaudhary Ld. LAC for the Accused: Sh. Mohd. Shadan CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 2 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 15:59:51 +0530 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Ms. Usha Rani (hereinafter referred to as "the Complainant") against Ms. Shaista Khan (hereinafter referred to as "the Accused"), under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant and the accused are known to each other since several years. That, accused and her husband were engaged in the business of Boutique and Beauty Parlour and in order to expand their business, the accused took Rs. 3,00,000/- from the committee which was headed by the complainant. That, the accused failed to deposit the monthly amount with the head of the committee/ complainant due to her financial losses. That, in the month of February, 2010, the complainant in order to help the accused, arranged an amount of Rs.2,60,000/- in cash from her neighbors and friends and the accused promised to return the said amount as earliest and possible. B. That, on repeated requests of the complainant, the accused had issued two cheques bearing no. 027027 dated 05.12.2012 for an amount of Rs. 2,00,000/- and no. 013643 dated 05.12.2012 for an amount of Rs. 60,000/-, both drawn at HDFC Bank Ltd., B-105, Chitranjan Park, New Delhi-110019 in favour of the complainant and in CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 3 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 15:59:57 +0530 discharge of his legal liability to pay the amount to the complainant and she assured the complainant that the cheque would be honored at the time of its presentation. C. That, on assurance of the accused person, the complainant had presented the aforesaid cheques for encashment with his banker namely Punjab National Bank, Alaknanda, New Delhi, however the cheques were returned dishonoured with the remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide returning memos dated 07.12.2012. D. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through his counsel, dated 15.12.2012, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheques within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at her correct address on 21.12.2012. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused has deliberately and willfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the complainant examined herself on affidavit being Ex. CW1/1 and placed on record Original Cheques in question is exhibited Ex. CW1/A & Ex. CW1/B respectively; Cheques return memos Ex. CW1/C & Ex. CW1/D respectively; Legal demand notice dt.15.12.2012 Mark-E; Courier Receipt and Proof of Delivery Ex. CW1/F & Ex. CW-1/G respectively. Further, in the pre- summoning evidence, complainant examined Sh. Hasibuddin as CW-2 who testified CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 4 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:03 +0530 that he had issued legal notice dated 15.12.2012 Mark-E on behalf of the complainant to the accused. 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused person was summoned. 5. Upon the appearance of the accused, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon her on 18.12.2015 to which she pleaded not guilty. At this stage, the accused admitted that she had issued the cheques in question and also admitted her signatures therein. She has denied receiving the legal demand notice. She stated that she was the member of the committee with the complainant, who took a cheque of Rs.60,000/- as security on the first occasion and after she made payment of the first committee, she also became member of second committee. She further stated that on asking of the complainant, she had given another cheque of Rs. 2,00,000/- as security for the second committee to the complainant. She further stated that the complainant had assured her to return both the cheques in question but she did not return the same despite accused making payments of both the above said committees and instead misused the same. 6. CW-1 Ms. Usha Rani/ complainant was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereby, CE was closed on 18.10.2022. Accordingly, matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused. 7. Statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 05.11.2022 wherein the accused opted to lead defence evidence. An application u/s 315 CrPC was moved on behalf of the accused for examination of CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 5 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:08 +0530 accused and Sh. Chandra Prakash Sharma as defence witnesses which was allowed by this Hon'ble court in the interest of justice vide order dated 02.12.2022. Accused examined herself as DW-1 and was examined, cross-examined and discharged. Sh. Chandra Prakash Sharma was examined as DW-2, cross-examined and discharged. DE was closed vide order of this court by recording a separate statement of the accused on 21.07.2025. 8. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 9. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 6 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:14 +0530 V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. 10. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 7 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:18 +0530 not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 11. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheque, i.e., bearing no. 027027 dated 05.12.2012 for Rs. 2,00,000/- and cheque bearing no. 013643 dated 05.12.2012, both drawn on HDFC Bank, CR Park (Ex. CW1/A & Ex. CW1/B). In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has admitted that the cheques in dispute belong to her. It is also not disputed that the cheques in question are not drawn on the account maintained by the accused person and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheques. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 12. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 8 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:24 +0530 banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheques in question were returned vide return memos dated 07.12.2012 (Ex. CW1/C & Ex. CW1/D) due to the reason "Funds Insufficient." By implication thereof, the cheques were presented within three months and the same were returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 13. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 15.12.2012 (Mark E) was dispatched on 17.12.2012 vide Courier (Ex. CW1/F), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has denied the receiving of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. However, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 14. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 9 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:30 +0530 15. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 16. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 10 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:37 +0530 (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 17. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 18. In the present case, in order to discharge her initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/1 and placed on record documents mentioned hereinbefore. The primary defence of the accused is that she had issued both the cheques in question as security for the committees which were handled by the complainant and that despite making the entire payment for the committee, the complainant has misused the present cheques in question. The accused has been consistent in her defence at the stage of notice u/s 251 CrPC, statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC and at the stage of DE. 19. The case of the complainant is that the accused received the lump sum of Rs. 3,00,000/- of the committee and after that failed to pay remaining installments of the CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 11 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:43 +0530 committee due to financial crisis, which is when the complainant arranged the sum of Rs. 2,60,000/- in good faith to help the accused and the accused has failed to repay the same. On being questioned about the financial capacity of the complainant to advance the sum of Rs. 2,60,000/- to the accused, the complainant in her cross-examination as CW-1 has stated that she had advanced the sum of Rs. 2,60,000/- to the accused by collecting money from neighbours and friends. The complainant has stated as follows: "I have no source of income except rental income..." "...I receive about Rs. 40,000/- per month as a rent from the above stated property. I used to collect a rent about Rs. 38,000/- per month in the year 2009-10..." "..I cannot tell whether I have mentioned in my ITR about the fact that I had collected money from my neighbours and friend to lend the money to the accused as mentioned in para no. 11.." "....I arranged amount of Rs. 2,60,000/- to be advanced to the accused from one Raj Rani and Dinesh however I do not remember of other persons from whom I arranged the aforesaid amount to be advanced to the accused by way of cash.." "...I took Rs. 15,000/- from Ms. Raj Rani and Rs. 15,000/- from Mr. Dinesh and balance amount was arranged from some other person and CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 12 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:48 +0530 myself. I do not remember the date, month and year in which I advanced Rs. 2,60,000/- to the accused...." "...I also did not mention any time period for returning of Rs. 15,000/- each to Dinesh and Raj Rani..." "...Slowly and steadily I returned the amount of Raj Rani, Dinesh and other persons from whom I had arranged the loan amount. I returned the loan of Raj Rani, Dinesh and other persons after receiving of cheque in question..." From the above, it is clear that the complainant did not have the financial capacity to extend the loan the loan to the accused and she is unable to bring forth any oral or documentary evidence to indicate how she collected the money to advance the loan to the accused. 20. In APS Forex Service Private Limited vs Shakti International Fashion Linkers , AIR 2020 SC 945, the Hon'ble Apex Court observed that: - "When the proceedings were initiated under Section 138 of the N.I. Act the accused denied the debt liability and the accused raised the defence and questioned the financial capacity of the complainant. To that, the complainant failed to prove and establish his financial capacity. Therefore, this Court was satisfied that the accused had a probable defence and consequently in absence of complainant having failed to prove his financial capacity, this Court acquitted the accused. In the present case, the accused never questioned the financial capacity of the CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 13 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:00:54 +0530 complainant. We are of the view that whenever the accused has questioned the financial capacity of the complainant in support of his probable defence, despite the presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act about the presumption of legally enforceable debt and such presumption is rebuttable, thereafter the onus shifts again on the complainant to prove his financial capacity and at that stage the complainant is required to lead the evidence to prove his financial capacity, more particularly when it is a case of giving loan by cash and thereafter issuance of a cheque." Similarly, in K. Subramani vs. K. Damodar Naidu , (2015) 1 SCC 99, it was observed that: - "In the present case the complainant and the accused were working as Lecturers in a Government college at the relevant time and the alleged loan of Rs.14 lakhs is claimed to have been paid by cash and it is disputed. Both of them were governed by the Government Servants' Conduct Rules which prescribes the mode of lending and borrowing. There is nothing on record to show that the prescribed mode was followed. The source claimed by the complainant is savings from his salary and an amount of Rs.5 lakhs derived by him from sale of site No.45 belonging to him. Neither in the complaint nor in the chief- examination of the complainant, there is any averment with regard to the sale price of site No.45. The concerned sale deed was also not produced. Though the complainant was an income-tax assessee he had admitted in his evidence that he had not shown the sale of site No.45 in his income- tax return. On the contrary the complainant has admitted in his evidence CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 14 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:01:00 +0530 that in the year 1997 he had obtained a loan of Rs.1,49,205/- from L.I.C. It is pertinent to note that the alleged loan of Rs.14 lakhs is claimed to have been disbursed in the year 1997 to the accused. Further the complainant did not produce bank statement to substantiate his claim. The trial court took into account the testimony of the wife of the complaint in another criminal case arising under Section 138 of the N.I. Act in which she has stated that the present appellant/accused had not taken any loan from her husband. On a consideration of entire oral and documentary evidence the trial court came to the conclusion that the complainant had no source of income to lend a sum of Rs.14 lakhs to the accused and he failed to prove that there is legally recoverable debt payable by the accused to him. In our view the said conclusion of the trial court has been arrived at on proper appreciation of material evidence on record. The impugned judgment of remand made by the High Court in this case is unsustainable and liable to be set aside." Therefore, in cases in which the impugned loan transaction is in cash, the accused can raise a probable defence by questioning the financial capacity of the complainant, and once the said question is raised, the onus shifts on the complainant to prove his financial capacity. In the present case, admittedly, no documents were placed on record to show that the complainant was having sufficient funds with her to advance such a huge loan amount. Further, such a huge loan was provided by the complainant to the accused without obtaining any receipt or any other document in this regard and this cannot be equated with the conduct of a prudent man acting in similar circumstances. Moreover, the complainant stated that she had borrowed CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 15 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:01:07 +0530 money from Raj Rani, Dinesh and some other individuals, however neither Raj Rani, Dinesh nor any other individual was ever examined as CW to corroborate the case of the complainant. This further substantiates and supports the argument of the accused that the accused was not in the financial capacity to advance the loan, as no prudent person would lend such a big sum to a stranger without any documentation or legally binding agreement. 21. Furthermore, the complainant was unaware of the material facts of the case, for instance, the complainant stated in her cross-examination as CW-1 that she does not remember her expenses at the time of advancement of the alleged loan and who she borrowed the money from to advance the loan to the accused or the date on which the loan was advanced to the accused. In the case of John K. Abraham v. Simon C. Abraham & Ors. , Supreme Court of India, 2013, the Hon'ble Apex Court had observed while dismissing the case of the complainant u/s 138 , NI Act: "The Respondent was not even aware of the date when substantial amount of Rs. 1,50,000/- was advanced by him to the Appellant, that he was not sure as to who wrote the cheque, that he was not even aware when exactly and where exactly the transaction took place for which the cheque came to be issued by the Appellant....." In the present case as well, the complainant has made several contradictory statements about how she arranged the sum to advance the loan to the accused as discussed above. It is an established law that contradiction of a witness's statement CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 16 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:01:17 +0530 on crucial aspects of a case would totally discredit their account and render it unreliable and untrustworthy. Furthermore, the conduct of the complainant with respect to advancing such a big sum of money by borrowing from individuals and not mentioning about the loan in her ITR and not obtaining any security regarding the said loan does not seem to be a conduct of a prudent person. 22. Moreover, the complainant has not brought either Raj Rani or Dinesh or produced any proof that she borrowed the sum from them to advance the loan to the accused. On the other hand, the accused brought DW-2 Sh. Chandra Prakash Sharma who stated that he was present alongwith Abid Ansari when the accused went to the complainant for return of her cheques as she has cleared the entire payment of the committee, to which the complainant stated that the cheques have been misplaced. The same is stated by the accused in her defence at the stage of legal notice u/s 251 CrPC, statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC and DE, thereby corroborating the version of the accused. 23. In view of the aforesaid findings and analysis, this court has arrived at an irresistible conclusion that the accused has been able to cast a shadow of reasonable doubt upon the case of the complainant by rebutting the mandatory presumption resting in its favour and by several inconsistencies in the version of the complainant. Once the accused had created a probable defence as to the legally enforceable liability, the onus shifted on the complainant to prove the existence of legally enforceable liability of the accused, as on the date of the drawal or presentation of the impugned cheques, which has not been fulfilled by the complainant in the present case. Since this basic ingredient which is pivotal to attract liability under Section 138 CC No. 619337/2016 Usha Rani Vs. Shaista Khan 17 of 19 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.28 16:01:23 +0530 NI Act has not been proved by the complainant, accordingly, no offence of dishonour of the impugned cheque under the said Section is made out. 24. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has not been fulfilled in the present case. Conclusion: 25. In view of the aforesaid discussion, the accused Ms. Shaista Khan has been successful in establishing a probable defence on a standard of preponderance of probabilities to rebut the presumption under Section 118 and 139 of the NI Act by punching holes in the case of the complainant and making the case of the complainant doubtful. The accused has been successful in establishing a probable defence and as a consequence, questioning the existence of legally enforceable liability in favour of the complainant and that the cheque was not issued by the accused in discharge of existing legally enforceable debt or liability owed to the complainant. In the result of the analysis of the present case, the accused Ms. Shaista Khan is hereby acquitted of the offence punishable under Section 138 , Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
